newsitem.title: UK: British police battle protesters in central London.
newsitem.headline: British police battle protesters in central London.

text.p: Environmental activists battled with police in riot gear in central London on Saturday after a march calling for greater social justice turned violent.

Police said at least four officers were injured when demonstrators bombarded them with cans, paint, sticks and smoke bombs at the entrance to Prime Minister John Major's official residence in Downing Street.
Several arrests were made as police donned protective clothing and called in reinforcements on horseback.
The protesters were forced back to Trafalgar Square where the main bulk of the marchers had arrived peacefully for a rally highlighting disparities in living standards.
Early in the evening, police were involved in a series of running skirmishes with some of the protesters, mounting baton charges against a hail of bottles and other ammunition.
A police spokeswoman said protesters were breaking up paving stones and using the pieces as missiles.
One man emerged from the melee with blood pouring from his face.

Police had sealed off the streets around Trafalgar Square to prevent any more people from joining the rally, which was mostly festive with marchers holding "Reclaim the Streets" banners dancing to music blaring from loud speakers.
They said around 1,500 people remained packed into the square.
Some protesters managed to drape huge banners reading "Trees Not MPs" and "Reclaim Your Environment" above the Canadian High Commission and the National Gallery.

A police spokeswoman said trouble began when a group of about 500 activists among the estimated 7,000-strong march harangued police standing behind barriers and then tried to climb the gates leading to Downing Street a few hundred metres (yards) south of Trafalgar Square.
Eyewitnesses said windows were broken in a nearby McDonalds hamburger restaurant and animal rights activists chanted slogans outside.

The march, organised by dockers from the north-west port of Liverpool who were sacked in a long-running industrial dispute, included hundreds of unemployed, disabled people, pensioners and aslyum seekers.

"Reclaim the Streets", one of several "direct action" groups that have emerged in Britain over the past five years, had warned it planned a "spectacular event" during the march and police had been on alert for trouble.
The group last year succeeded in closing one of the main highways into London and holding a two-day street party on it.
